subtopic_detail: Recurrent falls in an older person whose medication list carries a heavy anticholinergic and sedative load
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing an 82 year old woman admitted after her third fall in four months, this time with a wrist fracture. She lives alone and has become fearful of walking outside.

Her medications are oxybutynin for urge incontinence, temazepam nightly for twenty years, amitriptyline 25 mg at night for sleep, perindopril, atorvastatin and pantoprazole. Her lying blood pressure is 136/78 mmHg falling to 112/64 mmHg after three minutes standing, with no symptoms. Her pulse is 74 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air and temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius. Her sodium, calcium, renal function, vitamin D, full blood count and thyroid function are all normal, her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a normal corrected QT interval, and a cognitive screen shows mild impairment in attention and recall. Her visual acuity and footwear have been assessed and are satisfactory.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 136/78 mmHg lying and 112/64 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Slow unsteady gait with wide base, timed up and go 18 seconds, dry mouth, no focal neurological deficit, cognitive screen showing impaired attention and recall
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 72 nmol/L (50-150), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What intervention is most likely to reduce her risk of further falls?

options.text: A structured plan to withdraw the oxybutynin, amitriptyline and temazepam, with a progressive strength and balance programme
options.rationale: These three drugs carry the highest falls attributable risk on her list through anticholinergic burden, sedation and postural instability, and withdrawal combined with exercise has the strongest evidence for preventing further falls. Tapering rather than stopping abruptly is essential after twenty years of benzodiazepine use. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Commence a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and refer her to the fracture liaison service
options.rationale: Bone protection after a minimal trauma fracture is clearly indicated and should happen, but it reduces the consequence of the next fall rather than its likelihood. The question is which intervention reduces falls. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor for the cognitive impairment, and refer her for occupational therapy assessment
options.rationale: Her attention and recall deficits are most plausibly caused by the anticholinergic and sedative load rather than by a degenerative dementia, and treating them with a cholinesterase inhibitor while continuing oxybutynin sets one drug against another. Cognition should be reassessed after withdrawal. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Reduce the perindopril dose and add fludrocortisone, treating the drop in standing blood pressure as the cause
options.rationale: A fall of 24 mmHg systolic without symptoms does not meet the definition of orthostatic hypotension, and adding a mineralocorticoid brings oedema, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension for no established benefit. Her postural change is a distractor rather than the driver. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Substitute an alternative benzodiazepine with a shorter half life, and refer her for home hazard assessment
options.rationale: All benzodiazepines increase falls and a shorter half life does not remove that risk, while the substitution signals that the drug class is acceptable to continue. Home hazard assessment is useful but has modest effect as a standalone measure. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

explanation.summary: Falls in older people are multifactorial, and the assessment covers gait and balance, vision, footwear, cognition, continence, home hazards, orthostatic blood pressure, and medications. Among these, medication review is the element most often neglected and among the most effective, because the drug classes implicated are prescribed for symptoms that seem minor. Anticholinergic agents such as oxybutynin and amitriptyline impair attention, cause dry mouth and blurred vision and add directly to cognitive load, while benzodiazepines impair postural reflexes and reaction time with a risk that persists no matter how long the person has taken them. Withdrawal must be planned and gradual, particularly for benzodiazepines after years of use, with an alternative offered for the symptom that prompted the original prescription. The strongest evidence for falls reduction combines this deprescribing with a progressive strength and balance programme delivered for several months.
key_points: Anticholinergics and benzodiazepines are the highest yield targets on the list
Long standing use does not confer tolerance to the falls risk
Taper benzodiazepines gradually rather than stopping abruptly
Combine deprescribing with a progressive strength and balance programme
Bone protection reduces fracture severity but not the frequency of falls
explanation.pearls: Offer a specific alternative for the symptom that earned each drug its place, such as bladder training and a topical oestrogen for urge incontinence or sleep restriction therapy for insomnia, because deprescribing that leaves the original complaint unaddressed is the commonest reason a stopped medication reappears on the list within six months.

sources.label: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

subtopic_detail: Choosing a mood stabiliser for a young woman when the current agent carries teratogenic risk
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been well for eighteen months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, started during an inpatient admission for mania two years ago.

She has a new partner, uses no contraception, and tells you she would like to start a family within the next year or two. She has had one manic episode and two depressive episodes, has never self harmed, and has had no episodes since valproate was started. Her full blood count, liver function and weight are stable, and she takes no other medication. She asks whether she can simply stop the valproate when she decides to try to conceive.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood, normal speech and thought form, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, body mass index 26 kg/m2, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the valproate dose now and continue at that level, on the basis that the risk is dose dependent
options.rationale: The risk is indeed dose related but remains substantially above background at any effective dose, so dose reduction trades relapse risk for a residual teratogenic risk. It does not resolve the problem and leaves her on the drug. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.text: Continue valproate with high dose folate, and stop the valproate as soon as a pregnancy test becomes positive
options.rationale: Neural tube closure is complete by day 28 after conception, so stopping at a positive test is nearly always too late, and folate does not mitigate the malformation risk of this drug. This plan describes the exposure pattern the pregnancy prevention requirements exist to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.text: Continue valproate with a long acting reversible contraceptive, and revisit the medication when she actively conceives
options.rationale: Reliable contraception is necessary while she remains on the drug, but deferring the switch means it must occur under time pressure, and a rushed change risks relapse in early pregnancy. Planned switching while well is the whole purpose of the pre pregnancy conversation. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Stop valproate now without a replacement, and monitor her mood monthly given eighteen months of stability
options.rationale: Withdrawal of a mood stabiliser in bipolar I disorder carries a high relapse rate within the first year, and a manic relapse in pregnancy or the postpartum period is itself dangerous. Stability on treatment is not evidence that treatment is unnecessary. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Plan a cross taper from valproate to an alternative mood stabiliser now, with reliable contraception during the change
options.rationale: Valproate carries a roughly 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation and impairs neurodevelopment in around a third of exposed children, and the damage occurs in the first weeks before most pregnancies are recognised. Switching in a planned way while she is well and protected is far safer than stopping abruptly at a positive test. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic of the commonly used psychotropic drugs, with a major malformation rate of around 10 percent and neurodevelopmental impairment including reduced verbal intelligence and an increased rate of autism spectrum disorder in roughly a third of exposed children. Australian regulatory advice is that it should not be used in women or girls of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, and then only with a documented discussion and effective contraception. The practical failure is timing: organogenesis is largely complete before a woman knows she is pregnant, so a plan that depends on stopping at a positive test does not work. In a woman who is well and planning a family, the safer sequence is a planned cross taper under contraceptive cover to an agent with better pregnancy data, such as lamotrigine for a predominantly depressive course or an atypical antipsychotic such as quetiapine, with lithium considered where its benefit outweighs a small cardiac risk.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformation in around 10 percent of exposed pregnancies
Neurodevelopmental harm affects roughly a third of exposed children
Stopping at a positive pregnancy test is too late for neural tube closure
Switch in a planned way while well and under contraceptive cover
Do not stop a mood stabiliser without a replacement in bipolar I disorder
explanation.pearls: Document the pregnancy prevention discussion and the contraceptive method at every review for any woman of childbearing potential taking valproate, since the Australian requirement is a recorded annual discussion, and the absence of that documentation is what turns a foreseeable harm into an indefensible one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline
Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Fever and tachycardia in the third week of titration with a normal neutrophil count
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 27 year old man who is on day 19 of clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia, now taking 250 mg daily.

Over the past two days he has felt feverish and tired, with a temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius, pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and SpO2 97 percent on room air. He has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash, and his chest is clear. His neutrophil count is 4.8 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 96 mg/L, and troponin is elevated at six times the upper reference limit. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation. His psychotic symptoms have improved substantially on this dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no murmur, no rash, no focal infective source, mild ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 4.8 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), troponin six times the upper reference limit, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the clozapine at a reduced dose and repeat the troponin and C reactive protein in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Myocarditis from this drug is a hypersensitivity phenomenon rather than a dose dependent toxicity, so dose reduction does not remove the stimulus. Forty eight hours of continued exposure is how a reversible myocarditis becomes a cardiomyopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance

options.text: Cease the clozapine immediately and start filgrastim, treating this as a haematological adverse reaction
options.rationale: His neutrophil count is entirely normal, so there is no agranulocytosis to treat, and filgrastim carries its own risks. The fixation on the blood count is the trap, because monitoring on this drug is so strongly associated with neutrophils. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance

options.text: Cease the clozapine immediately and arrange urgent echocardiography with cardiology review
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, a raised C reactive protein and a rising troponin in the second to fourth week of titration describe clozapine induced myocarditis, which is the commonest cause of early death on this drug. The drug is stopped at once because continuing it during myocarditis can be fatal. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance

options.text: Continue the clozapine and treat with intravenous antibiotics for a presumed occult bacterial infection
options.rationale: There is no infective source and the troponin rise is not explained by sepsis, so treating for infection alone leaves an inflamed myocardium exposed to the causative drug. Cultures should still be taken, but the drug cannot continue while this is the leading diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance

options.text: Continue the clozapine and prescribe regular paracetamol, treating this as the benign fever seen during titration
options.rationale: A benign transient fever does occur during titration, but it is not accompanied by a troponin rise, and using that label here discards the one result that distinguishes the two. The troponin is the discriminating investigation. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, but it carries a distinctive set of serious adverse effects and the monitoring culture around it is dominated by neutrophil counts. Myocarditis is the complication most likely to be missed, typically occurring between days 14 and 28 of treatment, and Australian units generally monitor troponin and C reactive protein weekly through the first month for this reason. The presentation is non specific, with fever, tachycardia, fatigue, breathlessness or flu like symptoms, which is why isolated fever during titration is so often attributed to the known benign transient fever. A troponin above twice the upper reference limit, or a C reactive protein above 100 mg/L, prompts immediate cessation and echocardiography. Rechallenge after confirmed myocarditis is possible in specialist centres but requires cardiology involvement and very slow titration.
key_points: Myocarditis typically appears between days 14 and 28 of treatment
Weekly troponin and C reactive protein through the first month detect it
Symptoms are non specific and overlap with benign titration fever
Cease the drug immediately and arrange echocardiography
A normal neutrophil count does not exclude a serious adverse reaction
explanation.pearls: Ask about any new fever or breathlessness at every review in the first six weeks and check the troponin rather than relying on the patient volunteering symptoms, because sedation and negative symptoms both blunt reporting and the early presentation can be no more than tiredness and a resting pulse that has risen by 20 beats per minute.

subtopic_detail: Selecting cessation pharmacotherapy for a heavy smoker with stable treated depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 47 year old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for thirty years and lights his first cigarette within five minutes of waking.

He has recurrent major depressive disorder, well controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily for three years, with no episode in that time and no suicidal ideation ever. He has tried nicotine patches alone twice and relapsed within a fortnight both times. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, drinks four standard drinks weekly, and his renal function is normal. He asks which medication gives him the best chance and whether any of them are risky given his depression.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, chest clear, no signs of chronic lung disease
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy would you first recommend?

options.text: Behavioural support alone through a telephone quit service, with pharmacotherapy reserved for a later attempt
options.rationale: Counselling roughly doubles quit rates but combining it with pharmacotherapy is substantially better still, and withholding medication from a heavily dependent smoker is not justified by his psychiatric history. Support and medication are complementary. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Varenicline started a week before his quit date, with behavioural support and review at two and four weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for cessation, and the large randomised safety trial found no excess of neuropsychiatric events in people with stable treated psychiatric illness. Heavy dependence with failed patch monotherapy makes the most effective option the right first recommendation. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Nicotine patch monotherapy at the highest available strength, with behavioural support and review at two weeks
options.rationale: This is the approach that has already failed him twice, and repeating it with a higher dose does not address the reason it failed. Escalating within a strategy that has not worked wastes another quit attempt. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement using a patch with an oral form, with behavioural support and review at two weeks
options.rationale: Combination replacement clearly outperforms the patch alone and is a legitimate option, but head to head evidence still favours varenicline in heavily dependent smokers. It is the alternative if he declines the more effective agent. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation

options.text: Bupropion started a week before his quit date, with behavioural support and review at two and four weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but less so than varenicline, and it lowers the seizure threshold and interacts with serotonergic agents. It is a reasonable second line where varenicline is not tolerated. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation

explanation.summary: Smoking remains the leading preventable cause of death in Australia and people with mental illness smoke at two to three times the rate of the general population, yet are offered cessation treatment less often, partly because of longstanding concern about neuropsychiatric harm from varenicline. The large randomised trial comparing varenicline, bupropion, nicotine patch and placebo in people with and without psychiatric disorders found no significant excess of moderate or severe neuropsychiatric events attributable to either active drug, and Australian and international regulators subsequently removed the boxed warning. Varenicline is the most effective single agent, followed by combination nicotine replacement and bupropion, and all are more effective when combined with behavioural support. Time to first cigarette within thirty minutes of waking indicates high dependence and predicts a greater need for pharmacotherapy. Stopping smoking also raises the plasma levels of several psychotropic drugs, which matters for clozapine and olanzapine in particular.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for cessation
Stable treated psychiatric illness is not a contraindication to varenicline
Time to first cigarette within thirty minutes indicates high dependence
Combination nicotine replacement beats patch monotherapy
Pharmacotherapy plus behavioural support outperforms either alone
explanation.pearls: Remember that tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2, so stopping smoking raises clozapine and olanzapine levels by up to half within a week or two, and a patient stabilised on clozapine who quits without a dose review can become toxic with sedation, hypersalivation and seizures.

subtopic_detail: Slowly declining kidney function after more than a decade of maintenance treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for fourteen years with excellent mood stability and no admissions in that time.

His estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 52 mL/min/1.73m2 over the past five years, with the most recent two readings three months apart both at 52 and 54. His twelve hour post dose lithium level is 0.78 mmol/L, urine albumin to creatinine ratio is normal, his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, and renal ultrasound shows normal sized kidneys with no obstruction. He passes large volumes of dilute urine and drinks accordingly. He takes no non steroidal anti inflammatory medication and no diuretic, and he is euthymic with no current symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no ataxia, normal reflexes, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 52 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 78 over five years), twelve hour lithium level 0.78 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), urine albumin to creatinine ratio normal, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.52 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium immediately and substitute sodium valproate, given the fall in kidney function over five years
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal carries a substantial risk of rebound mania within weeks, and this degree of impairment does not demand emergency cessation. Any change should be gradual and planned rather than driven by a single trajectory. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Continue lithium at a lower target level with nephrology review, and discuss the long term options with him
options.rationale: Progression to end stage disease is uncommon and slow, while stopping lithium after fourteen years of stability carries a high risk of relapse and of refractoriness if it is later restarted. Shared decision making with nephrology input, aiming at the lowest effective level, is the recommended approach at this stage. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Add a thiazide diuretic for the polyuria and continue lithium at the current dose and target level
options.rationale: Thiazides reduce lithium clearance and raise the level, which is the opposite of what is needed here, and the polyuria of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is treated with amiloride if treatment is required at all. This choice risks toxicity on top of impairment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Change the dosing to twice daily at the same total dose, and repeat kidney function in twelve months
options.rationale: Divided dosing produces a higher trough exposure and is associated with more renal effect than once daily dosing, so this moves in the wrong direction. Single evening dosing is generally preferred for that reason. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Continue lithium unchanged and repeat kidney function annually, since he remains well and the level is in range
options.rationale: A fall of 26 mL/min/1.73m2 over five years is a meaningful trajectory rather than expected ageing, so continuing without adjustment or specialist input misses the window in which the rate of decline can be modified. Monitoring needs to become more frequent, not less. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long term treatment in bipolar disorder and the only one with good evidence for reducing suicide, so decisions about renal effects are genuinely a balance rather than a simple stop or continue. Chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy develops slowly over decades and appears as a gradual decline in filtration with preserved urinary protein and normal sized kidneys, often alongside nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from impaired collecting duct responsiveness. Progression to end stage kidney disease occurs in well under 1 percent of treated patients. Risk is increased by episodes of toxicity, by dehydration, by concurrent non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and thiazides, and by divided rather than single daily dosing. Management of a declining filtration rate is joint review with nephrology, minimising the effective level, avoiding nephrotoxic combinations, and an explicit conversation about the relapse risk of stopping, since psychiatric relapse also carries mortality.
key_points: Decline is slow and end stage disease occurs in well under 1 percent
Preserved urinary protein with normal sized kidneys is the typical picture
Single daily dosing is preferred over divided dosing
Thiazides, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and anti inflammatories raise levels
Abrupt cessation risks rebound mania and later refractoriness
explanation.pearls: Check the corrected calcium as well as thyroid function at every annual review, because lithium causes hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia in up to a quarter of long term users, and the resulting fatigue, low mood and cognitive slowing are routinely misread as a depressive relapse and treated with an antidepressant.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline
